ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The sphenoid bone sits at the skull base, forming part of the sella turcica and orbit walls. Its complex shape supports the pituitary gland and provides corridors for cranial nerves and vessels. Understanding its relations helps diagnose skull base lesions and plan neurosurgical approaches.

sections.p: The sphenoid is a butterfly‑shaped bone central to the skull base, articulating with many other bones and housing the pituitary fossa.
b: Central, butterfly shape; articulates with ethmoid, occipital, temporal, parietal, frontal, and maxillary bones.

sections.p: It has a body, greater and lesser wings, pterygoid processes, and a central sella turcica that cradles the pituitary.
b: Body: central core; wings: lateral extensions; pterygoid processes: posterior projections; sella turcica: pituitary pit.

t.b: Shows bone erosion or mass effect; indicates possible tumor or infection.

sections.p: Anteriorly, it contacts the nasal cavity and maxillary sinuses; posteriorly, it meets the clivus and foramen magnum. The optic chiasm lies just above its superior surface.
b: Optic chiasm, pituitary stalk, internal carotid arteries, cavernous sinus, cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, VI pass nearby.

t.b: Defines soft tissue mass and optic nerve compression.

sections.p: The sphenopalatine artery, middle meningeal artery, and branches of the internal carotid supply the bone and adjacent structures.
b: Sphenopalatine artery: nasal cavity; middle meningeal: dura; internal carotid: cavernous sinus.

t.b: Detects vascular tumors or aneurysms involving the sphenoid.

sections.p: Sensory fibers from the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of V, and motor fibers to the pterygoid muscles.
b: V1 and V2 sensory; pterygoid muscles motor via V3.

t.b: Loss of facial sensation or jaw deviation suggests pterygoid involvement.

sections.p: Provides a central base for the skull, supports the pituitary gland, and forms part of the orbit and nasal cavity.
b: Supports pituitary; forms orbital floor; contributes to nasal cavity floor.

t.b: Assesses hormonal imbalance due to pituitary compression.

sections.p: Lesions such as pituitary adenomas, chordomas, or infections can erode the sphenoid, causing visual loss, cranial nerve palsies, or endocrine dysfunction.
b: Pituitary adenoma: mass effect; chordoma: bone destruction; osteomyelitis: infection; trauma: fractures.

t.b: Detects bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression.

sections.p: Remember the sphenoid’s role as a central hub: it houses the pituitary, supports the optic chiasm, and is a corridor for cranial nerves and vessels. Masses here often present with visual changes and endocrine symptoms.
b: Masses → visual loss, endocrine signs; fractures → cranial nerve deficits; infections → fever, headache.

t.b: Best for bone erosion and mass delineation.
Best for soft tissue and nerve involvement.

whenToSeekHelp: Massive visual field loss, sudden headache with neck stiffness, or signs of pituitary dysfunction such as amenorrhea or adrenal insufficiency.

faq.q: What symptoms suggest a sphenoid bone lesion?
faq.a: Visual disturbances, cranial nerve palsies, headaches, and endocrine changes.

faq.q: How is a sphenoid fracture diagnosed?
faq.a: CT scan shows bone discontinuity and possible displacement.

faq.q: Why is MRI preferred for pituitary tumors?
faq.a: It provides superior soft tissue contrast and shows optic nerve compression.

exam: Describe the anatomical relations of the sphenoid bone and explain why a pituitary adenoma can cause bitemporal hemianopia.
Explain the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected sphenoid bone osteomyelitis.
Discuss management options for a sphenoid wing fracture in a low‑resource setting.
